analysis.one_liner: Stops credit bureaus from selling mortgage applicants' information to other lenders without their permission.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House by voice vote, cleared the Senate without objection, and was signed into law on September 5, 2025, with 89 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: When you apply for a mortgage, credit bureaus have been allowed to sell your credit report to other lenders and mortgage brokers, who then call or text you with competing offers — these are called 'trigger leads.' The law makes that illegal in most cases: a bureau can only share your report with a third party if that party can show you actually agreed to be contacted, or if it already has a relationship with you — it originated or services your current mortgage, or it is a bank or credit union where you have an existing account. It takes effect 180 days after enactment and directs the Government Accountability Office to study trigger leads sent by text message.
analysis.who_benefits: People applying for a residential mortgage, who gain privacy and a break from the flood of unsolicited calls and texts triggered by their own credit application.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a credit reporting agency from furnishing a consumer's report to a third party in connection with a residential mortgage transaction unless it is a firm offer of credit and the third party certifies the consumer's authorization, or has an existing relationship with the consumer (originated or services their mortgage, or holds their account at a bank or credit union).
Takes effect 180 days after enactment, so the protection applies to mortgage applications beginning in early 2026.
Requires a GAO study of trigger leads received by text message, with input from state regulators, lenders, bureaus, and consumers, reported to Congress within a year.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer reporting agencies lose the revenue they earn from selling mortgage trigger leads, and lenders and brokers who rely on purchased leads lose a marketing channel. The exception for banks and credit unions with an existing account for the consumer leaves them a channel independent lenders do not get.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves an exception for insured depository institutions and credit unions that already hold a consumer's account, so large banks can still trigger contact without fresh consent while independent mortgage brokers and nonbank lenders cannot — tilting the market toward banks.

Supporters of trigger leads argue they generate competing offers that can lower borrowers' rates; eliminating them may reduce price competition, which the bill acknowledges only indirectly by ordering a GAO study on the value of one lead channel.
The restriction applies only to credit transactions involving residential mortgage loans; trigger leads tied to auto loans, credit cards, and other credit applications remain legal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gain for mortgage applicants is real and targeted, and the cost falls almost entirely on the credit bureaus and lead buyers rather than on consumers. The main weakness is the carve-out that favors banks over independent lenders, which softens but does not erase the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee unanimously, passed the House under a fast-track procedure with no roll call, passed the Senate by unanimous consent, and was signed by the President on September 5, 2025.

narrative.text: The House Financial Services Committee approved the amended bill 46-0 on June 10, 2025, and reported it June 20.
The House passed it by voice vote on June 23, 2025, under suspension of the rules, a fast-track procedure reserved for noncontroversial bills.
The Senate passed it without amendment by unanimous consent on August 2, 2025.
The President signed it on September 5, 2025, making it Public Law 119-36.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage applicants, who will stop getting their information sold after they apply for a loan; the banks-and-credit-unions carve-out also leaves them better positioned relative to independent lenders.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support before it reached the floor.

for.name: President of the United States
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on September 5, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: Support split across party lines with no recorded opposition: the committee voted 46-0, 89 cosponsors included 33 Democrats and 56 Republicans, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and the House took no recorded vote against it.

industries.note: Bureaus lose the revenue from furnishing mortgage trigger leads to third parties, the practice this law restricts; that loss is what gives mortgage applicants their privacy back.

They lose the ability to buy trigger leads without a consumer's certified authorization, removing a lead-generation channel, though competing offers from them could also have benefited borrowers through rate competition.

The law's exception lets an insured depository institution or credit union that already holds the consumer's account keep receiving mortgage trigger leads without fresh consent — a channel independent lenders do not get, steering mortgage traffic toward banks.
